client: Hi, I'm feeling a bit overwhelmed today. It's like I'm juggling too many things and nothing is settling.
therapist: Juggling many things can indeed feel overwhelming. It's important to find moments where you can pause and reconnect with what matters most. What aspects of your day have been particularly demanding, and how might we work together to help them feel more manageable?

answer_final: I'm sorry to hear that. What is the cause of your anxiety?
client: You're right, taking a moment could really help. I feel anxious because everything's moving so fast, and I'm afraid I'll drop the ball.
therapist: Taking that moment can truly ground you. Let's explore what might help slow things down and support your sense of balance. What small steps could we consider to ease the pace and reassure you in these challenging times?

user: My friends and my family place a lot of value on how one looks. Every time I meet with them they have a comment on how I should improve on something. It makes me stressed out because I feel like I am not good enough.
answer_final: I am sorry you are having to deal with this. Are you concerned about your own looks because you constantly hear this feedback from those close to you?
client: It'd be helpful to find a way to pause when those moments get stressful. Lately, the comments from my friends and family about my appearance amplify that stress. I'm worried their opinions make me doubt myself.
therapist: It's challenging when outside opinions affect your self-view. Let's explore ways to bolster your confidence during these stressful times. What supportive actions or thoughts could help affirm your own worth and ease the influence of others' comments?

user: Yes. I feel that I am not thin enough, pretty enough, that my clothes are not nice enough etc
answer_final: I myself have gone through similar feelings when I was a teenager. I had body image issues for the longest time and my way of resolving it was through proper diet and exercise. Are you happy with how you look personally irrespective of what others opinions are?
client: I think I’ve let their words define how I see myself—like my weight, looks, even my style aren’t good enough. It’s hard to separate their opinions from my own.
therapist: Your willingness to explore this is commendable. You deserve to define yourself beyond others' opinions. How can you reconnect with the aspects of your identity that truly resonate with you and affirm your self-worth?

user: It is hard to feel ok when I keep hearing that I am missing something. I don't even think I need to lose weight. It is just that my friends think model thin is what beauty is. I would have to starve myself to achieve that.
answer_final: If you are comfortable with your weight then why are you so concerned with what everyone around you says or thinks?
client: It's hard to stay confident when constantly hearing that I'm lacking something. I don't think weight loss is needed for me, but my friends idolize model thinness as beauty, which feels unattainable without harming myself.
therapist: Striving to meet unattainable ideals can feel exhausting and unkind. How has this pressure from your friends impacted your relationship with yourself, and what might you want to reclaim as your own definition of beauty or well-being?

user: Because they are the people I spend time with. I want to be accepted and I want them to like me.
answer_final: It sounds like you care more about what others think of you than how you feel about yourself.
client: I spend so much time with them, craving acceptance. It's exhausting, and I've started doubting my self-worth. I need to redefine beauty on my terms.
therapist: You deserve acceptance for who you truly are. This external pressure can be named as the "beauty ideal critic." How would embracing your unique definition of beauty impact your sense of self-worth and ease your need for others' approval?

user: I wish I could not care about what they think but I do. I don't know how to not let their opinions not bother me
answer_final: Have you ever tried affirmations or heard of this before?
client: I think embracing my own definition of beauty would feel freeing, but it’s hard to let go of their opinions. Their judgments still weigh heavily on me, even though I wish they didn’t.
therapist: Finding freedom in your own definition of beauty is such a powerful intention. What small, supportive step could you take to start lightening the weight of their judgments and nurture your sense of self-worth?

answer_final: Affirmations are positive statements you think about yourself. What I like to do when I'm feeling really anxious is say three positive things/attributes I feel about myself over and over again until my anxiety dissipates. Do you think that could help you feel more positively about what those closest to you are saying so much with regards to looks?
client: I'm not entirely sure what steps to take, but maybe I could start by setting boundaries or spending less time in those judgment-heavy conversations. It feels intimidating, though.
therapist: Taking those steps can feel daunting, but exploring boundaries is a brave start. What matters most to you as you consider shifting these conversations? Small, steady changes might begin easing this burden while honoring your own values and needs.

user: I could try. Do I need to say positive things about my looks or can they be about other stuff?
answer_final: Since you are stating that you are concerned about how you look, you should just find a few positive statements with regards to your looks you think about yourself and repeat them. So if you don't think you need to lose weight, you can say something like, "I like my weight." or "I don't need to lose weight." If you think you are beautiful or pretty, you can say "I am beautiful." My three affirmations I use for myself are: I am beautiful, smart, and funny. I say this over and over again until my anxiety has left me.
client: I think starting with small changes might help, like shifting focus to what I value about myself—not just looks. Could it include strengths or things I’m proud of?
therapist: Shifting focus to your strengths and what you’re proud of feels like a meaningful step. What’s one quality or achievement that stands out to you—a part of yourself you deeply value and want to celebrate?

user: That sounds easy enough. I will definitely try it. It will take my mind off of worrying about what they are thinking.
answer_final: I highly recommend it! Is there anything else bothering you that I can help with?
client: One quality that stands out is my ability to connect with people. It brings me joy, and focusing on this will help shift my thoughts from worrying about their opinions.
therapist: Focusing on your ability to connect with others and the joy it brings is a wonderful shift. How might celebrating this quality further strengthen your self-worth, separate from external opinions?

user: No you gave me a great suggestion to work with. Thank you so much for your help!
answer_final: No problem! Glad I could help. I hope you have a wonderful day and take care!

client: Reflecting on these interactions, I realize they often affirm the kindness and warmth I value in myself. Thanks for helping me see that. Goodbye for now.
